title: Were You There
description: The spiritual as Hampton Institute's singers sang it, for 2 to 4 singers: the soprano asks each verse's question alone, the others echo her under her held note, and everyone sings the rest in harmony, through "Sometimes it causes me to tremble" to the question once more. Four verses. Slow and quiet.

credits.words: traditional spiritual, as sung at Hampton Institute (published 1909)
credits.tune: traditional spiritual, as sung at Hampton Institute (published 1909)

licence.arrangement: original, written for Stackapella (the printed four-part setting, by Hampton Institute's unnamed musical directors, used only to check the chords). Accepted exceptions (singable.py): the tune's own line "when they cru-ci-fied" on D, D, E, D, D (the licence: the print's upper treble voice, as it is sung today), almost 5 seconds at the top of the beginner soprano range in each verse; and the alto's fourth from B on "there?" (and on the same question's last word in verses 2 to 4) up to E on "Were" comes across the breath into a new line, after which it climbs with the tune's own arpeggio a third under it, G under B on "you" and B under D on "there", so it does not step back.
licence.source: tune and words from R. Nathaniel Dett, ed., Religious Folk-Songs of the Negro as Sung at Hampton Institute (Hampton Institute Press, Hampton, Va., 1927), Appendix p. VI, "Were You There When They Crucified My Lord?" (Dett died 1943), which reprints the setting of Religious Folk Songs of the Negro as Sung on the Plantations, new edition arranged by the musical directors of the Hampton Normal and Agricultural Institute (The Institute Press, Hampton, Va., 1909), p. 162; in G, 4/4, Adagio con molto espress., quarter = 68, as printed and as written here; verses 1 to 4 of the 5; in the tutti "Were you there when they crucified my Lord?" the melody is the print's upper treble voice (D D D E D D), the tune as it is sung today, with the lower parts our own, and "Oh!" holds the upper voice's D, leaving out its turn up to G5; the fermatas of "trem-ble, trem-ble" are held, so that bar has 8 beats; read from the scans at archive.org/details/religiousfolkson00dett and archive.org/details/religiousfolkson00hamp
